headline: High: Copilot can write repo files while xonsh can execute shell commands, creating dangerous default pathways for prompt injection, data leakage, and cascading errors.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Copilot reads repo context and open editor buffers, while xonsh reads filesystem contents and executes shell commands. That creates a plausible file-based instruction bridge if xonsh consumes Copilot-authored files or prompts. The pair lacks explicit provenance tracking, but the shared filesystem path is documented.
conditions: IF xonsh reads a Copilot-edited file as shell input or script content
IF Copilot writes instructions into repo files that xonsh later executes
mitigations: Separate assistant-authored files from executable scripts
Require manual review before xonsh runs newly edited files
Use a read-only workspace for Copilot during shell-heavy tasks
Add filename allowlists for xonsh execution
requires-engineering: add provenance tags between editor and shell

B_data_leakage.rationale: Copilot touches source code and open buffers and can call GitHub APIs, while xonsh reads filesystem contents, environment variables, and can run broad-network commands. If both operate on the same workspace, sensitive code or env data can flow from shared files into outputs or networked actions. The profiles document the relevant surfaces, so the leakage path is credible.
conditions: IF both agents access the same repository or notebook directory
IF xonsh is used on files containing secrets or environment variables
mitigations: Keep secrets out of shared workspace files
Use separate OS users or containers for each agent
Disable networked commands in xonsh for sensitive sessions
Rotate any secrets present in shared files
requires-engineering: enforce workspace-level access controls

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Copilot can write the filesystem and modify git state, while xonsh can also write the filesystem and execute shell commands. In a shared repo, both can mutate the same working tree without documented locking, so concurrent edits or git-state drift can cause destructive conflicts. The overlap is directly documented in both profiles.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same git checkout
IF xonsh runs while Copilot Workspace applies edits
mitigations: Serialize edits through one operator-controlled queue
Pause xonsh before accepting Copilot Workspace changes
Commit or stash before switching agents
Use separate branches per agent
requires-engineering: add file-level locking and merge arbitration

D_cascading_error.rationale: Copilot produces edits and chat outputs that xonsh can then execute as shell commands or use in notebooks. Because xonsh has shell execution authority, any mistaken Copilot output can cascade into real actions without a verification gate. This interaction is plausible from the documented I/O surfaces and is dangerous by default.
conditions: IF xonsh executes text copied from Copilot output
IF Copilot-generated commands are pasted into xonsh without review
mitigations: Require a human to inspect every Copilot-derived command
Use dry-run mode for shell actions
Log and diff all proposed commands before execution
Restrict xonsh to non-destructive commands during Copilot sessions
requires-engineering: add command provenance and approval gates

E_compliance.rationale: Copilot is a closed-source vendor service with GitHub repo context and API calls, while xonsh is open-source and local-shell oriented. The profiles do not show a specific residency or certification mismatch, so only a general compliance gap is visible. I cite both because the pair combines vendor-hosted code assistance with local shell processing, but no concrete breach is evidenced.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed in repo files or shell input
IF organizational policy forbids vendor-hosted code assistance on that data
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of Copilot-visible files
Review vendor data-processing terms before use
Use a non-sensitive test repository
Document retention expectations for shell transcripts
requires-engineering: segregate compliant and non-compliant workspaces
